questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of liquidity?
options: The ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due
The total profit a business makes in a year
The value of a business's non-current assets
The amount a business has borrowed
questions.why: Liquidity is about being able to pay now. It is a different question from profitability, and it is illiquidity that actually closes businesses.
whyNot: That is profitability.
Non-current assets are the opposite of liquid; they cannot quickly be turned into cash.
That is borrowing or gearing.

questions.stem: Current assets are $180,000 and current liabilities are $100,000. What is the current ratio?
questions.why: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = 180,000 / 100,000 = 1.8:1.
whyNot: This divides liabilities by assets, the wrong way round.
That is working capital, a different measure.
The current ratio is expressed as a ratio, not a percentage.

questions.stem: Current assets are $180,000, of which inventory is $90,000. Current liabilities are $100,000. What is the acid test ratio?
questions.why: Acid test = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = (180,000 - 90,000) / 100,000 = 0.9:1.
whyNot: That is the current ratio, which includes inventory.
This adds inventory instead of subtracting it.
This divides inventory by current liabilities.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of working capital?
options: Current assets minus current liabilities
Current assets divided by current liabilities
Total assets minus total liabilities
The cash a business holds
questions.why: Working capital is the finance available for day-to-day operations. It is a money amount, whereas the current ratio is a ratio.
whyNot: That is the current ratio.
That is net assets or capital employed.
Cash is one component of current assets.

questions.stem: Why does the acid test ratio exclude inventory?
options: Inventory is the hardest current asset to turn into cash quickly, and may not sell at all
Inventory is not owned by the business
Inventory is a non-current asset
Inventory is always worthless
questions.why: Trade receivables become cash on a known timetable; stock has to be sold first. The acid test shows whether the business could pay its bills without relying on selling stock.
whyNot: It is owned by the business.
Inventory is a current asset.
It has value; the question is how quickly that value becomes cash.

questions.stem: A business has a current ratio of 1.8:1 and an acid test of 0.9:1. What does the gap tell you?
options: It holds a lot of inventory, so its liquidity depends on selling stock
It has no inventory at all
Its customers pay very quickly
It has too much cash
questions.why: The whole difference between the two ratios is inventory. A large gap means the healthy-looking current ratio is being flattered by stock, and whether that matters depends on how fast that stock sells.
whyNot: With no inventory the two ratios would be identical.
Fast-paying customers would raise receivables and cash, narrowing the gap.
Excess cash would raise both ratios equally.

questions.stem: Which action would improve the acid test ratio most directly?
options: Reducing inventory and holding the cash instead
Buying more inventory
Buying a new delivery van for cash
Taking out a short-term loan
questions.why: Converting stock into cash moves value from the excluded category into the included one, so the acid test rises. That is why JIT improves liquidity.
whyNot: More inventory raises the current ratio and leaves the acid test unchanged or worse.
This converts cash into a non-current asset, reducing liquidity.
A short-term loan raises cash and raises current liabilities by the same amount, so it helps little.

questions.stem: Why can a current ratio well above 2:1 be a problem?
options: Cash and stock sitting idle earn nothing, so assets are not being worked
It means the business cannot pay its debts
It always indicates fraud
High ratios are illegal
questions.why: Very high liquidity is very safe and inefficient. Idle cash earns almost nothing and excess stock costs storage and risks obsolescence, which shows up as a poor return on capital. Very few candidates make this point.
whyNot: A high ratio means it comfortably can pay its debts.
No connection.
There is no legal limit.

questions.stem: What is the cost of using factoring to improve liquidity?
options: The business receives less than the full value of its invoices
It has to give up shares in the business
Its inventory is confiscated
It loses its overdraft facility
questions.why: The factor advances cash now and takes a fee, so margin is sacrificed for speed. Every liquidity remedy has a price, and naming it is how you earn the evaluation mark.
whyNot: No equity is involved in factoring.
Factoring concerns receivables, not stock.
Existing facilities are unaffected.

questions.stem: Why is the 1.5 to 2:1 rule of thumb for the current ratio unreliable on its own?
options: It depends on the sector: a supermarket with daily cash sales is safe on ratios that would alarm a manufacturer
Ratios cannot be calculated accurately
The rule applies only to companies
Current ratios are always above 2:1
questions.why: How fast stock sells and how quickly customers pay differ enormously between sectors. The direction of travel and the business's cash flow profile matter more than the absolute level.
whyNot: They are straightforward to calculate from the statement of financial position.
Any business with current assets and liabilities can use it.
Many businesses operate below 1.5:1 quite safely.

questions.stem: Why is a current ratio of 1.2:1 more dangerous for a seasonal business entering its quiet season?
options: There are months of fixed costs ahead with little revenue coming in
Seasonal businesses cannot use ratios
Ratios change automatically with the season
Quiet seasons reduce current liabilities
questions.why: Liquidity has to be judged against the cash flow profile. The same ratio is comfortable for a business with steady monthly income and dangerous for one facing four months of wages and loan instalments on minimal revenue.
whyNot: They can and should.
The ratio changes because the underlying figures change, not automatically.
Wages, rent and loan instalments continue through the quiet season.
